I was down roughly -$60K going into college, already 2+ years into trading.

I could've decided I wasn't cut out for it. Instead, I kept studying, journaling, losing, adjusting + showing up. Now I'm entering year 6+ and still have an absurd amount to learn.

I think 1 of the hardest things for newer traders to accept is that some lessons simply require time.

Someone can explain risk management to you 100 times...then you oversize one trade, get absolutely smoked, and suddenly you understand it differently. Someone can tell you not to chase...then you chase enough extended stocks and finally understand why. Someone can preach patience...then you spend months overtrading chop and realize doing nothing would've made you more money (hence the last 3 months).

Failure isn't wasted time if you're extracting the lesson from it.

That's literally trading summed up into simple terms.

Everyone wants the breakthrough, but very few people want the boring Tuesday night reviewing 37 losing trades to figure out why they keep making the same mistake. Unfortunately, that's usually where the breakthrough is hiding.

Put in the reps.

It’s awfully quite in here nowadays, at least that’s my own observation.

And I get it, market has been tough, this is a market that has punished chasers, trapped buyers, shaken out traders at logical levels, only to rip higher again without them.

And if you are too aggressive in opening up exposure, you bleed for every new ”bullish change of character” that occurs.

Zooming out we see a market deteriorating under the hood, the kind of deterioration that will lead to a large directional move lower if not resolved soon, that can be a bleed down. Everybody always assume we crash, we can chop downwards as well.

But weekly structure is still in favor of the bulls, if breadth and broad equity bid resumes.

In the end we don’t have to guess the direction, we can assess the market conditions as supportive or non supportive for swingtrading. And currently it is simply mixed, some things working, most things roundtripping, selective groups are outperforming excessively, which is also a sign of unhealth.

Because it’s Capital hiding in the only few things that’s working. What follows is usually a big rug pull if real weakness continues.

If trading has been tough, it won’t get better by being aggressive at the wrong time, there are no shortcuts. Risk management -> real progressive exposure -> wait for traction that is sustained to push the gas.

We get 1-2 times a year with breadth this bad, these low readings can fuel multimonth trends WHEN we turn. But timing is critical, what good will the trend be for you, if you burned yourself in crappy trades during chop before the burst higher. 

Slow and steady wins the game, maximum flexibility, market read and risk management skills required in this tape.

Nobody knows where we are heading, this is the time to focus and pay attention.

5 Ways to Improve Your Market Performance — by the late Van K. Tharp, Ph.D. 

1. Invest with the current trend of the market.

"Before entering the market, know what the market is doing. Is it going up or down?

Look at the $SPY and compare its price with the 200-day moving average. When the market is above its 200-day moving average, it has historically performed better than when it is below it.

The 200-day moving average can help keep you on the right side of the major market trend. If prices break below it, consider reducing your exposure."

2. Never enter a position without knowing where you will get out.

"Before entering any position, determine your exit point.

The investment industry often promotes “buy and hold,” but holding without an exit plan can expose you to major losses. If you don’t know where to get out, you don’t know your risk."

Tharp suggested a 25% trailing stop as a minimum for long-term positions, giving a position room to trend while providing protection against a major decline.

3. Never risk more than 1% of your portfolio on any position.

"Position size should be determined by your risk, not by how much you want to buy.

If you have a $25,000 portfolio, risking 1% means limiting your potential loss to $250 on any position. If your stop is $2 away, you can buy 125 shares. If your stop is $20 away, you can buy only 12 shares.

The position size changes, but the portfolio risk remains the same.

Stay safe to live long enough in the markets so you can learn and improve."

4. Continually observe your patterns, habits and emotions.

"Self-awareness is essential to improvement.

Pay attention to what you are thinking and feeling when entering, managing and exiting trades. Keep a trading journal and look for recurring emotions, thoughts and behaviours that may be hurting your performance.

The goal is not to eliminate emotions, but to become aware of them without allowing them to control your decisions."

5. Take responsibility for your results.

"It is easy to blame the market, your broker, analysts, fund managers or external events when things go wrong.

But avoiding personal responsibility prevents you from learning from your mistakes.

If you take full accountability for your results, you can identify what went wrong, correct it and avoid repeating the same mistakes.

No matter what happens in the market, take responsibility for your results. That’s how you learn and improve."

A few people asked how I even had ~$60K to lose that young + how I built myself back after losing it.

I was the weird high school kid running meme pages & building accounts on Instagram. By sophomore year, I had a million+ followers across different pages, and eventually turned that skill into a small social media agency where I helped businesses/clients grow their accounts.

That was really my first taste of entrepreneurship, and it gave me capital WAY earlier than I probably had the maturity to know what to do with.

A few mentors told me, “You need to do something with this money.” So naturally, being young and thinking I knew everything, I discovered the stock market and proceeded to do something with it alright...I lost roughly $60K in my first 2 years trading penny stocks & 0dte options.

That hole was brutal emotionally because I knew how many hours of work went into earning that money in the first place. There were plenty of moments where quitting would've been way easier than admitting I simply hadn't built the skill yet.

But I've never really been wired to quit something because I'm bad at it.

I kept working, kept earning outside the market, kept studying charts, and kept putting reps in while trying to understand why I was failing.

Year 3 was probably the biggest inflection point for me.

I stopped trying to be every type of trader, gravitated heavily toward swing trading, found mentors, simplified what I was looking for + finally started building a system around my own personality. That's when consistency slowly started showing up because I finally started recognizing my strengths, admitted my weaknesses, and started building rules around both.

Now I'm heading into year 6+, and I still fail ALL the time. The difference is that failure doesn't scare me nearly as much anymore because I've seen what can happen when I refuse to waste the lesson.

Social media gave me my first capital. Trading took a lot of it away, but the process of earning it back + becoming a better trader completely changed my life.

Forever grateful for the markets...and I genuinely feel like I'm just getting started. I hope this inspires someone to never give up on what you've started.

1 piece of advice: Fall in love with the process, and always bet on yourself.
